newsitem.title: PERU: Shell ups 1997 budget for Peru's Camisea 25 pct.
newsitem.headline: Shell ups 1997 budget for Peru's Camisea 25 pct.

text.p: Royal Dutch/Shell has increased this year's budget for Peru's Camisea project by 25 percent to $125 million, mainly to invest in studies for a gas pipeline to Lima, a company official said.

Shell, which is the operating partner in the Camisea project with a 57.5 percent share in a consortium with Mobil, originally budgeted this year to invest $100 million in drilling three appraisal wells in the huge reserves in Peru's eastern jungle.

"Really this extra investment takes us into the start of the development stage," Shell Prospecting and Development (Peru) B.V. Managing Director Alan Hunt told Reuters in Nuevo Mundo, the supply base near the Camisea fields.

Shell and Mobil signed a contract with the government last year that gives them the rights for two years to appraise Camisea's reserves with a view to developing them. The reserves are estimated to hold 11 trillion cubic feet of natural gas and 600 million barrels of natural gas liquids.
Shell is working with two foreign groups chosen to submit proposals for the development of a project to bring gas 310 miles (500 km) to Lima from the Camisea fields.

The company has chosen a consortium of the United States' Bechtel, Peru's COSAPI and Brazil's Odebrecht, and another consortium of the United States' Fluor Daniel, Peru's Grana y Montero and Argentina's Techint to design a pipeline.
Shell has said it expects to award a contract for the detailed design of the proposed pipeline by mid-1997.
The Anglo-Dutch oil firm also hopes to produce gas from the reserves as early as 1999 and to bring gas to Lima in the full development project around 2002.

Shell is already working to establish a market for its gas among industrial companies in Lima. "In an ideal world we should sign contracts for the purchase and supply of gas this year," Hunt said in the interview conducted on Wednesday..

Last month, Shell started drilling its first appraisal well in the Cashiriari field. It plans to move the rig in June to a second field, San Martin, and back to a fresh site in the Cashiriari field 100 days later.

The first well, which deviates 30 degrees from the perpendicular, has already reached a depth of around 2,500 meters (2,734 yards) out of a planned total depth around 2,850 meters (3,116 yards), drill-site manager James Wells said.
If the oil consortium decides to exploit the reserves, the project will last 40 years and become the largest foreign investment commitment in Peru at up to an estimated $3.0 billion.
The fields hold six times the rest of the country's reserves, according to the government, which estimates it will receive $6 billion in tax revenue from the project during the first 30 years.
